description:
from objectstore import FileIOResolver, HttpClient, S3Client

Modules: `http` (a libcurl-backed client, because no Mojo HTTP package
resolves from conda), `crypto` (SHA-256/HMAC, because nothing provides them
and SigV4 is made of them), `sigv4`, `path` (URI handling), `fileio` (the
`InputFile`/`OutputFile`/`FileIO` traits and the scheme resolver), `local`,
`ranges` (coalescing many byte ranges into few requests), `httpio`, `s3`, and
— over SAS/bearer URLs only — `gcs` and `azure`.

modules.summary: `objectstore.azure` — Azure Blob Storage through SAS-token URLs.
modules.description:
Azure's own signing schemes are `SharedKey` (an HMAC-SHA256 over a canonical
form that is close to but not the same as SigV4) and Entra ID bearer tokens.
Neither is implemented. What is implemented is the **SAS token**: a query
string that already carries a signature someone else produced, which is what
Iceberg's `adls.sas-token.<account>` property holds and what a catalog vends.
With a SAS token, a blob is an HTTPS URL, and the whole backend is URL
construction plus two required headers.

Iceberg addresses ADLS Gen2 as `abfss://container@account.dfs.core.windows.net/path`.
The Blob endpoint (`account.blob.core.windows.net`) serves the same data with
the simpler API, so that is what this targets; `wasbs://` names the Blob
endpoint directly and is accepted as well.

aliases.name: BLOB_API_VERSION
aliases.summary: Sent as `x-ms-version`. Azure requires it on every request, and older services reject versions they do not know — this one is old enough to be universally supported and new enough for everything used here.

structs.name: AzureLocation
structs.summary: A parsed `abfs(s)://` or `wasb(s)://` location.

fields.name: sas_token
fields.summary: The query string of a SAS URL, with or without its leading `?`.

fields.name: endpoint
fields.summary: Overrides the derived `https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net`, for Azurite or a sovereign cloud.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, var account: String, var sas_token: String, var endpoint: String)
def from_properties(props: Dict[String, String], account: String = "") -> Self
overloads.summary: Reads Iceberg's `adls.sas-token.<account>` (and a plain `adls.sas-token` / `azure.sas-token` fallback).

overloads.signature: def url_for(self, container: String, blob: String) -> String
def list_url(self, container: String, prefix: String, marker: String) -> String
def __init__(out self, var config: AzureConfig, var http: HttpClient)
def input(self, container: String, blob: String) -> HttpInputFile
def output(self, container: String, blob: String) -> HttpOutputFile
def delete_blob(self, container: String, blob: String)
def list_blobs(self, container: String, prefix: String = "") -> List[BlobInfo]
overloads.summary: Every blob under `prefix`, following `NextMarker` pages.
overloads.description:
The response is `<EnumerationResults><Blobs><Blob><Name>…`, which the
same shallow XML reader handles as S3's `ListBucketResult`.

overloads.summary: `abfss://container@account.dfs.core.windows.net/a/b` -> account `account`, container `container`, path `a/b`.
overloads.description:
`wasbs://container@account.blob.core.windows.net/a/b` parses the same way.
A bare `az://container/path` is accepted with the account left empty, for
callers that configure the endpoint explicitly.

modules.summary: `objectstore.crypto` — SHA-256, HMAC-SHA256 and hex, in pure Mojo.
modules.description:
AWS SigV4 is built entirely out of these two primitives, and nothing in the
Mojo ecosystem provides either: hashes.mojo covers the *non-cryptographic*
hashes Iceberg needs for partition transforms (murmur3, xxhash, CRC32), and no
conda-resolvable package offers SHA-2. Rather than pull OpenSSL in through a
second FFI shim — libcurl already links it, but its EVP surface is a moving
target across conda builds — this module implements FIPS 180-4 and RFC 2104
directly.

SigV4 hashes the *whole* payload of every signed PUT, so this is not a
negligible cost: a purely scalar compression function caps a multipart upload
at the speed of the hash. The block loop therefore has three backends, chosen
at compile time by `_BACKEND`:

* `armv8-crypto` — the ARMv8 SHA-2 extension (`sha256h`/`sha256h2`/`sha256su0`
  /`sha256su1`), which every Apple Silicon and every server aarch64 part has.
* `x86-sha-ni`   — Intel SHA extensions (`sha256rnds2`/`sha256msg1`
  /`sha256msg2`), present on AMD Zen and on Intel from Goldmont/Ice Lake
  client onwards, but *not* on Ice Lake / Sapphire Rapids Xeons.
* `scalar`       — portable FIPS 180-4, fully unrolled with a 16-word rolling
  schedule so the whole working set stays in registers.

The choice is a `comptime` query of the *target's* CPU features, and `mojo`
compiles for the host CPU unless told otherwise, so on a normal build (pixi
source dependency, `pixi run`, CI) the compile-time answer is the run-time
truth. A binary deliberately cross-built with `--target-cpu` for a CPU it will
not run on is the one case that would fault, and that is the same contract as
every other `-march=native` build.

If a general-purpose home ever appears, this belongs in hashes.mojo.

structs.name: Sha256
structs.summary: Streaming FIPS 180-4 SHA-256.
structs.description:
Streaming rather than one-shot because a SigV4 `PUT` has to hash the whole
payload, which for a data file is larger than anything worth copying into
one contiguous buffer just to hash it.

overloads.summary: The digest of everything fed so far. Does not consume `self`, so a caller can keep hashing afterwards.
Which compression backend this build is using: `armv8-crypto`, `armv8-crypto (asm)`, `x86-sha-ni` or `scalar`. Benchmarks and tests print it so a CI log says which path it actually exercised.

The CPU features this build was compiled against, as the backend choice saw them. A `scalar` backend on hardware that plainly has the extension means `mojo` did not resolve the host CPU — this is the line that says so.
SHA-256 forced through the portable backend, whatever `_BACKEND` is.
overloads.description:
Exists so the test suite can cross-check the hardware path against the
reference implementation on the very machine that runs it — the two are
entirely separate code, and the FIPS vectors alone would not catch a
schedule bug that only shows up past the first block.

overloads.signature: def hmac_sha256(key: Span[UInt8], msg: Span[UInt8]) -> List[UInt8]
overloads.summary: RFC 2104 HMAC with SHA-256. Keys longer than the 64-byte block are hashed first; shorter keys are zero-padded.

overloads.signature: def hmac_sha256(key: Span[UInt8], msg: String) -> List[UInt8]
def hmac_sha256_hex(key: Span[UInt8], msg: String) -> String

overloads.summary: Lowercase hex — the case SigV4's canonical request requires.

modules.summary: `objectstore.fileio` — the `InputFile` / `OutputFile` / `FileIO` traits and the scheme resolver.
modules.description:
This is the seam iceberg.mojo already anticipates. Its `src/iceberg/io.mojo`
declares an `InputFile` trait with `location()`, `exists()` and `read_all()`,
and a local-only `FileIO`; the traits here are a **superset** of that, so an
`objectstore` input file satisfies the Iceberg trait unchanged, while adding
the two things a lazy Parquet reader needs: `length()` and
`read_range(offset, length)`.

`FileIOResolver` is the dynamic half. Mojo dispatches traits statically, so a
"pick a backend by URI scheme" API cannot return an arbitrary trait
implementation; `AnyInputFile` and `AnyOutputFile` are small tagged unions over
the three backends, and they conform to the traits themselves. Generic code can
keep using the traits; code that resolves locations at runtime uses the
resolver.

Per-scheme configuration follows Iceberg's property names (`s3.endpoint`,
`s3.access-key-id`, …) so a `LoadTableResult`'s `config` map can be handed
straight over, and `storage-credentials` — the REST spec's list of
`{prefix, config}` entries — is matched **longest prefix first**, exactly as
the spec requires when a catalog vends different credentials for different
paths within one table.

aliases.name: BACKEND_AZURE
aliases.summary: GCS and Azure reduce to `BACKEND_HTTP` once a location has been turned into a URL plus headers — a bearer token for GCS, a SAS query string and `x-ms-version` for Azure — so only the resolver distinguishes them. The open files themselves are `HttpInputFile`/`HttpOutputFile`.

structs.name: AnyInputFile
structs.summary: An `InputFile` whose backend is chosen at runtime by URI scheme.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, backend: Int, var uri: String, var local: LocalInputFile, var http: HttpInputFile, var s3: S3Client, var bucket: String, var key: String)
def read_range(self, offset: Int, length: Int) -> List[UInt8]

overloads.summary: One seek per range for local files. For HTTP and S3, nearby ranges are coalesced and the groups fetched at once.

structs.name: AnyOutputFile
structs.summary: An `OutputFile` whose backend is chosen at runtime by URI scheme.
structs.description:
The HTTP backend covers three cases that all reduce to a single `PUT`: a
presigned S3 upload URL, GCS's XML endpoint with a bearer token, and an
Azure blob with a SAS token. `create` there is "check, then write", which
is racy — HTTP has no atomic create.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, backend: Int, var uri: String, var local: LocalOutputFile, var http: HttpOutputFile, var s3: S3Client, var bucket: String, var key: String)

structs.name: StorageCredential
structs.summary: One entry of a REST `LoadTableResult`'s `storage-credentials`.
structs.description:
Same shape as `iceberg.catalog.rest.StorageCredential`, so a parsed
response can be forwarded without translation.

structs.name: FileIOResolver
structs.summary: Picks a backend by URI scheme and configures it from properties.
structs.description:
Property resolution for a given location, most specific first:

1. the longest matching `storage-credentials` prefix,
2. the resolver's own properties (an Iceberg table's `config`),
3. `AWS_*` environment variables.

Location rewrites (`rebase`) are applied before any of that, because
Iceberg metadata records absolute locations and a warehouse that has been
copied elsewhere — or a test fixture checked into a repo — needs them
redirected without rewriting the metadata.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, var properties: Dict[String, String])
def set(mut self, var key: String, var value: String)
def add_storage_credential(mut self, var prefix: String, var config: Dict[String, String])
def rebase(mut self, var old_prefix: String, var new_prefix: String)
overloads.summary: Redirect every location under `old_prefix` to `new_prefix`.
overloads.description: Byte-compatible with `iceberg.io.FileIO.rebase`.

overloads.summary: The location this one should actually be read from.

overloads.signature: def properties_for(self, location: String) -> Dict[String, String]
overloads.summary: Merged properties for one location, most specific last.
overloads.description:
`storage-credentials` entries are matched by prefix and the **longest**
match wins: a catalog may vend one credential for a table's data
prefix and a narrower one for a single partition, and the narrower
entry is the one that was meant.

overloads.signature: def azure_config_for(self, location: String, account: String) -> AzureConfig

overloads.summary: Locations under `prefix`, as full URIs.
overloads.description:
Local listing is recursive; S3 listing is flat by nature — an object
store has no directories, only key prefixes.

overloads.signature: def read_range(self, location: String, offset: Int, length: Int) -> List[UInt8]
overloads.summary: The bytes `[offset, offset+length)`.
overloads.description:
This is the entry point a lazy Parquet reader wants: fetch the last
64 KiB for the footer, then exactly the row groups the scan needs.

overloads.signature: def read_ranges(self, location: String, ranges: List[ByteRange]) -> List[List[UInt8]]
overloads.summary: Several ranges of one object, coalesced where that saves requests.
overloads.description:
One `new_input` for the lot, so an S3 location is signed and addressed
once rather than once per range.

overloads.summary: Several whole objects, in order. Those on S3 are fetched at once; the rest one by one. For many small files read together, such as an Iceberg table's manifests.

overloads.signature: def read_ranges_many(self, locations: List[String], ranges: List[List[ByteRange]]) -> List[List[List[UInt8]]]
overloads.summary: `ranges[i]` of `locations[i]`, for every `i`, in order.
overloads.description:
Each file's ranges are coalesced as `read_ranges` does, and then every
group of every file on S3 is fetched in one batch: reading several
files' footers, or several files' column chunks, costs one round of
requests rather than one per file. Other backends read file by file.

overloads.signature: def write(self, location: String, data: Span[UInt8])

traits.name: InputFile
traits.summary: A readable byte source addressed by a location.
traits.description:
`location`, `exists` and `read_all` are byte-compatible with
`iceberg.io.InputFile`; `length` and `read_range` are the additions that
let a reader fetch a Parquet footer without pulling the whole file.

overloads.signature: def read_range(self, offset: Int, length: Int) -> List[UInt8]

overloads.summary: Several ranges at once, in the order asked for.
overloads.description:
The default is one `read_range` per range, which is exactly right for
a file the process can seek. Backends where a range costs a round trip
override it to coalesce (see `objectstore.ranges`), which is what
turns a Parquet scan's per-column-chunk reads into a handful of
requests.

traits.name: OutputFile
traits.description:
`create` fails if the location already exists; `overwrite` does not. That
is Iceberg's own distinction — metadata files are written with `create` so
that two writers racing on the same version number cannot both believe
they won.

traits.name: FileIO
traits.summary: A namespace of locations: open, delete, list.

modules.summary: `objectstore.gcs` — Google Cloud Storage over the S3-compatible XML endpoint.
modules.description:
GCS exposes two APIs. The JSON API (`storage.googleapis.com/storage/v1/…`)
returns JSON, which would mean carrying a JSON parser here purely to read an
object listing. The **XML API** (`storage.googleapis.com/<bucket>/<key>`) is
byte-for-byte the S3 protocol for everything this tin does — `GET` with
`Range`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and a `ListBucketResult` document the S3 parser in
`s3.mojo` already reads. So this module uses the XML endpoint, and is
correspondingly small.

**Authentication is an OAuth2 bearer token supplied by the caller.** Minting
one from a service-account key requires RS256 JWT signing, and RSA is out of
scope — it is a great deal more code than SHA-256 was, for something
`gcloud auth print-access-token`, a metadata server, or the surrounding
application already has. Pass the token in as `gcs.oauth2.token`, which is
Iceberg's own property name for exactly this.

GCS also accepts SigV4 with HMAC "interoperability" keys; a caller who has
those can point `S3Client` at `https://storage.googleapis.com` instead.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, var endpoint: String, var oauth_token: String)

overloads.summary: Iceberg's GCS property names: `gcs.oauth2.token` and `gcs.service.host`.

overloads.signature: def url_for(self, bucket: String, key: String) -> String
def __init__(out self, var config: GcsConfig, var http: HttpClient)
def input(self, bucket: String, key: String) -> HttpInputFile
def output(self, bucket: String, key: String) -> HttpOutputFile
def delete_object(self, bucket: String, key: String)
def list_objects(self, bucket: String, prefix: String = "", delimiter: String = "", continuation_token: String = "") -> ListResult
overloads.summary: One page of the XML API's `ListBucketResult`.
overloads.description:
GCS implements S3's `list-type=2` continuation tokens, so the response
parses with `s3.parse_list_objects` unchanged.

overloads.signature: def list_all(self, bucket: String, prefix: String = "") -> ListResult

overloads.summary: `gs://bucket/a/b` -> `("bucket", "a/b")`. `gcs://` is accepted too.

modules.description:
**Why libcurl.** Nothing in the Mojo package ecosystem gives this repo a TLS
capable HTTP client: `floki`, `flare`, `lightbug-http` and `fire-http` all fail
to resolve from conda ("No candidates were found") on both the stable and the
nightly toolchain, and an object store without HTTPS is not an object store.
conda-forge's `libcurl` ships TLS and a CA bundle for every platform we target,
so this tin follows the magmalake FFI recipe (zstd.mojo, lz4.mojo): a tiny C
shim built as a `pixi-build-cmake` package into `$CONDA_PREFIX/lib`, found by
`_dlopen.open_library` (with or without `CONDA_PREFIX`) and dlopened once per
process through an `OwnedDLHandle`.

The shim exists because `curl_easy_setopt` is a C variadic, which a dlopened
symbol cannot express; `shim/curl_wrapper.c` collapses a whole request into one
fixed-arity call and hands back an opaque result object read through accessors.

Every FFI-calling worker takes the handle as a borrowed `imm` parameter: Mojo
destroys a value at its last syntactic use, so a function that both owned the
handle and called `get_function` on it would `dlclose` the library before the
returned function pointer is invoked.

**Connection reuse.** The curl easy handle lives in the shim and persists
across requests, so a second request to the same host reuses its TCP and TLS
session instead of shaking hands again — the difference between ~2.9 ms and
~0.2 ms per range read on loopback. Requests go to a process-wide pool by
default; `new_connection_pool` hands out a private one for a caller that wants
its connections kept apart.

**Threads.** Requests can be made from several threads at once (shim ABI
5): `SHARED_POOL` and a batch's multi handle are per thread in the shim, with
their own connections, and what threads share — DNS and TLS sessions — sits
behind locks.
A private pool from `new_connection_pool` belongs to one thread at a time.

**Batches.** `request_many` sends several requests at once and returns when
all have answered: one thread, curl's multi interface underneath, its own
persistent connections. A ranged read of a Parquet file is mostly waiting for
first bytes, so overlapping the waits is most of the speed there is to have.

**Retries.** Transport failures, 429 and most 5xx are retried with exponential
backoff and jitter, but only for requests that can safely be repeated — see
`RetryPolicy`. A response that is *returned* is never retried behind the
caller's back on a method the server might have already acted on.

aliases.name: DEFAULT_MAX_PARALLEL
aliases.summary: Requests a batch keeps in flight at once, on as many connections. The Rust Iceberg reader keeps 10 range reads in flight per file; S3 serves each connection at roughly 100 MB/s, so 16 covers a node's share of bandwidth without opening sockets by the hundred.

aliases.name: DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS
aliases.summary: Total request deadline. Range reads of a Parquet footer are small; a 20 MB object over a slow link is not, so this is generous rather than tight.

aliases.name: SHARED_POOL
aliases.summary: The process-wide connection pool, which is what every `HttpClient` uses unless it is given one of its own.

structs.name: Header
structs.summary: One `Name: Value` pair. Names are compared case-insensitively.

structs.name: RetryPolicy
structs.summary: When to try again, and how long to wait first.
structs.description:
Defaults: three retries (four attempts), 100 ms doubling to a 20 s ceiling,
and **idempotent requests only**. `POST` is retried only when the caller
has said the server can deduplicate it by supplying an `Idempotency-Key`
header — which is exactly what an Iceberg REST commit does, and why the
header is the trigger rather than a flag on the client.

fields.name: max_retries
fields.summary: Attempts *after* the first. 0 disables retrying entirely.

fields.name: retry_non_idempotent
fields.summary: Escape hatch for a caller that knows its `POST` is safe to repeat and cannot add a header. Off, because guessing wrong duplicates a write.

overloads.summary: One request, one answer — the 0.1.x behaviour.

structs.name: Response
structs.summary: A completed HTTP response: status line, headers, and the whole body.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, status: Int, var headers: List[Header], var body: List[UInt8])

overloads.summary: The first value for `name` (case-insensitive), or `""`.

overloads.signature: def body_excerpt(self, limit: Int = Int(256)) -> String
overloads.summary: The first `limit` bytes of the body, for error messages.
overloads.description:
S3 and Iceberg REST both answer errors with a short XML or JSON
document; truncating keeps a raised `Error` readable when the body is
a 20 MB object instead.

structs.name: BatchRequest
structs.summary: One request of a batch: a `GET` or `HEAD`, optionally ranged.
structs.description: `expect_len`, when known, sizes the response buffer up front.

overloads.signature: def get(var url: String, var headers: List[Header] = List(), range_start: Int = Int(-1), range_end: Int = Int(-1)) -> Self

structs.name: HttpClient
structs.summary: An HTTP client over a persistent, reused connection.
structs.description:
The client itself holds no socket: `pool` names a curl handle living in
the shim, and `SHARED_POOL` — the default — is the process-wide one. Two
`HttpClient` values therefore share connections, which is what makes an
Iceberg scan that opens a new `S3Client` per file cheap. With the default
pool, threads may each make requests at once.

Redirects are **off** by default: a presigned S3 URL carries its signature
in the query string and must never be silently re-issued elsewhere.

fields.name: pool
fields.summary: `SHARED_POOL`, or a handle from `new_connection_pool()` that the caller is responsible for freeing.

overloads.signature: def request(self, method: String, url: String, headers: List[Header] = List(), body: Span[UInt8] = Span(), range_start: Int = Int(-1), range_end: Int = Int(-1)) -> Response
overloads.summary: Performs the request, retrying per `self.retry`.
overloads.description:
Raises only on *transport* failure — a 404 or a 500 comes back as a
`Response` so the caller can decide. A retryable status that survives
the last attempt is returned too: the caller sees the server's own
answer rather than an invented error.

overloads.signature: def request_many(self, reqs: List[BatchRequest], max_parallel: Int = Int(16)) -> List[Response]
overloads.summary: Every request in `reqs` at once, answers in the same order.
overloads.description:
Like `request`, a status comes back as a `Response` and only a
transport failure raises. A request that failed in transport or got
a retryable answer is tried again on its own, under `self.retry`.
Batches are `GET`s and `HEAD`s, which are always safe to repeat. A
shim older than ABI 4 has no batches: then they run one by one.

overloads.signature: def get(self, url: String, headers: List[Header] = List(), range_start: Int = Int(-1), range_end: Int = Int(-1)) -> Response
def head(self, url: String, headers: List[Header] = List()) -> Response
def put(self, url: String, body: Span[UInt8], headers: List[Header] = List()) -> Response
def post(self, url: String, body: Span[UInt8], headers: List[Header] = List()) -> Response
def delete(self, url: String, headers: List[Header] = List()) -> Response

overloads.summary: A private pool: one persistent curl handle, its own connections.
overloads.description:
Returns an opaque handle to pass as `HttpClient.pool`. **The caller owns
it** and must call `free_connection_pool`; there is no destructor here
because `HttpClient` is `Copyable`, and a copyable owner of a C resource
is a double free waiting to happen. Most callers want `SHARED_POOL`.

overloads.summary: Closes a pool from `new_connection_pool` and its live connections.

overloads.signature: def pool_stats(pool: Int = Int(0)) -> Tuple[Int, Int]
overloads.summary: `(requests, connections)` for a pool since the last `reset_pool_stats`.
overloads.description:
`connections` is what curl actually opened, so reuse is the observation
that it stays at 1 while `requests` climbs — which is how the tests prove
it rather than inferring it from a stopwatch.

overloads.summary: 1 = a fresh curl handle per request (0.1.x); 2 = pooled connections; 3 = `instance_credentials_blob`; 4 = batches (`request_many`); 5 = safe from several threads.
The EC2 instance role's credentials, as the shim's IMDSv2 lookup hands     them back: `access-key-id secret token expiry-epoch`, or `""` when     there are none.
overloads.description:
The shim caches the answer for the process, "none" included, so this is
    cheap to call per request. A shim older than ABI 3 has no lookup and
    answers `""` as well.

overloads.summary: Headers as the shim wants them: `Name: Value` lines joined by LF.
overloads.description:
An HTTP header value cannot contain a bare LF, so this encoding is
lossless and spares the FFI boundary a `char*[]`.

overloads.signature: def is_idempotent(method: String, headers: List[Header]) -> Bool
overloads.summary: RFC 9110 idempotency, plus the `Idempotency-Key` convention.
overloads.description:
`GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS` and `TRACE` are idempotent by
definition: repeating one cannot commit a second effect. `POST` and
`PATCH` are not, so they are only repeatable when the request carries a
key the server can deduplicate on.

overloads.summary: 429 and 5xx, except the two that mean "never, no matter how often".
overloads.description:
501 Not Implemented and 505 HTTP Version Not Supported are permanent facts
about the server; retrying them is pure latency.

overloads.summary: S3's two "come back later" errors, which arrive with unhelpful statuses.
overloads.description:
`SlowDown` is throttling and `RequestTimeout` means the server gave up
waiting on the body; AWS returns the latter as a **400**, so status alone
would call it permanent. Only the first bytes are inspected, and only for
a response that already failed, so this never touches an object body.

overloads.signature: def backoff_delay_ms(policy: RetryPolicy, attempt: Int) -> Int
overloads.summary: Exponential backoff with jitter: half the window fixed, half random.
overloads.description:
`attempt` counts from 1. Full jitter would sometimes retry instantly and
hammer a server that is already asking for room; half is the usual
compromise. The jitter source is the monotonic clock's low bits — there is
no RNG in reach here, and a retry schedule does not need a good one.

overloads.summary: Parses curl's raw header text into pairs.
overloads.description:
curl emits one header block per response it sees, so a redirect chain or a
`100 Continue` produces several. Only the last block describes the
response the caller gets, so a new status line resets the accumulator.

overloads.summary: `(requests, connections)` for batches since `reset_batch_stats`: the connections stay few while requests climb, because batches reuse them.
Libcurl's own version banner, e.g. `libcurl/8.9.1 OpenSSL/3.3.1 …`.

modules.description:
Two things make this worth having beyond "download the file". A `HEAD` gives
the length without a body, and a `Range` request gives an arbitrary slice — so
a Parquet file published over plain HTTP is as lazily readable as one in S3.
And a **presigned S3 URL** is, at the point of use, just an HTTPS URL with a
signature in the query string: this is the backend that reads it, with no
credentials involved.

Servers are allowed to ignore `Range` and answer `200` with the whole body.
That is handled rather than trusted: a `200` where a `206` was expected is
sliced locally, so the caller always gets the bytes it asked for.

fields.name: headers
fields.summary: Sent with every request. This is what makes the module reusable for GCS (`Authorization: Bearer …`) and Azure (`x-ms-version`) — both reduce to an HTTPS URL plus a fixed set of headers.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, var url: String, var client: HttpClient)
def read_range(self, offset: Int, length: Int) -> List[UInt8]
overloads.summary: `length` bytes from `offset`. A negative `offset` is a suffix range (`bytes=-N`), the way HTTP itself spells "the last N bytes".
One request per *group* of nearby ranges rather than one per range.
overloads.description:
Connection reuse made a request cheap; this makes it rare. A Parquet
row group whose column chunks are laid out consecutively becomes a
single `Range` request, and the bytes of the columns the scan skipped
are read and thrown away — which is cheaper than the round trip that
would have avoided them. The groups are fetched at once.

structs.name: HttpOutputFile
structs.summary: A write-only file behind a single `PUT`.
structs.description:
Only usable where a plain `PUT` to a URL means "store this object" — a
presigned S3 upload URL, GCS's XML endpoint with a bearer token, an Azure
blob URL with a SAS token. It is not a general HTTP writer, because HTTP
itself has no create-versus-overwrite distinction: `create` is implemented
as "check, then write", which is racy and says so.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, var url: String, var headers: List[Header])
def http_delete(url: String, headers: List[Header], client: HttpClient)

modules.description:
Range reads use `seek` + `read_bytes(n)`, which Mojo's `FileHandle` supports,
so reading a Parquet footer out of a 2 GB file costs 64 KiB rather than 2 GB.
Everything else is a thin wrapper whose value is uniformity: the same
`InputFile`/`OutputFile` shape as S3 and HTTP, so a caller never branches on
where a table happens to live.

structs.name: LocalInputFile
structs.summary: A readable file at an ordinary filesystem path.

overloads.signature: def read_range(self, offset: Int, length: Int) -> List[UInt8]
overloads.summary: `length` bytes from `offset`; a short read at EOF is not an error.
overloads.description:
A negative `offset` counts back from the end, the way an HTTP suffix
range does — which is how a Parquet reader asks for a footer.

structs.name: LocalOutputFile
structs.summary: A writable file at an ordinary filesystem path.
structs.description:
Parent directories are created on demand: Iceberg writes to deep,
partition-shaped paths that no one has made in advance.

overloads.summary: Removes a file. A missing file is not an error — deletion is idempotent here for the same reason it is on S3.
Every file under `prefix`, recursively, as `file://` URIs.
overloads.description:
A prefix that names a file lists just that file, which keeps the contract
the same as S3's: a prefix is a prefix, not necessarily a directory.

overloads.summary: Opens a `file://` URI or a bare path.

modules.description:
Iceberg stores **absolute** locations everywhere: a table's `location`, a
snapshot's `manifest-list`, a manifest entry's `file_path`. Those strings are
the only addressing this stack has, so parsing them precisely — and rewriting
them when a warehouse is copied somewhere else — is a first-class concern
rather than string fiddling scattered across call sites.

Grammar handled here:

    s3://bucket/key/parts        object stores (s3, s3a, s3n, gs, gcs, abfs*, wasb*)
    https://host/path?query      HTTP(S), including presigned URLs
    file:///abs/path             a local file, RFC 8089 style
    file://host/abs/path         tolerated; the host is ignored
    /abs/path or rel/path        a bare filesystem path, scheme `file`

structs.name: Uri
structs.summary: A parsed location.
structs.description:
`bucket` is the authority: an S3/GCS bucket, an Azure container's account
host, or an HTTP host[:port]. `key` is everything after it with no leading
slash — which is exactly what an S3 request needs, and exactly what a
filesystem path needs once the leading slash is put back for `file`.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, var scheme: String, var bucket: String, var key: String, var query: String, var raw: String)

overloads.summary: The filesystem path for a `file:` URI.
overloads.description:
`file:///a/b` and `/a/b` both give `/a/b`; a relative bare path is
returned unchanged so `tests/fixtures/x` keeps working.

overloads.summary: The location rebuilt from its parts — round-trips `parse_uri`.

overloads.signature: def join(base: String, child: String) -> String
overloads.summary: Joins a location with a relative child. An absolute `child` wins.
The containing directory/prefix, with no trailing slash.
overloads.description:
`s3://b/a/b/c` -> `s3://b/a/b`; `s3://b/c` -> `s3://b`; a bare name with
no slash has no parent and yields `""`.

overloads.summary: `file:///a/b` -> `/a/b`; other schemes are returned unchanged.
overloads.description:
Kept byte-compatible with `iceberg.io.strip_scheme` so iceberg.mojo can
swap its copy for this one.

overloads.signature: def url_encode(s: String, encode_slash: Bool = True) -> String
overloads.summary: RFC 3986 percent-encoding of everything outside the unreserved set.
overloads.description:
SigV4 needs both variants: path segments keep `/` literal, query keys and
values do not (SigV4 §canonical query string).

modules.summary: `objectstore.ranges` — byte ranges, and the plan that turns many into few.
modules.description:
A Parquet scan does not read a file, it reads a list of spans: the footer,
then one span per column chunk of each row group it kept. Over local storage
that is a list of seeks and costs nothing. Over HTTP it is a list of *requests*,
and even with connection reuse each one still costs a round trip — so the
useful optimisation is not making requests faster, it is making fewer of them.

Column chunks of the same row group are laid out consecutively, which means the
spans a scan asks for are usually adjacent or separated by the columns it
skipped. Fetching across a small hole and throwing the hole away is cheaper
than a second round trip: this module works out where those holes are.

The bound is `max_gap` (1 MiB by default), applied per join, so the bytes read
and discarded are at most `max_gap` times the number of joins — never more than
the caller asked for plus that.

This module deliberately knows nothing about transports; `fileio` and `httpio`
execute the plan.

aliases.name: DEFAULT_COALESCE_GAP
aliases.summary: Holes up to this size are read and discarded rather than skipped. A MiB is roughly where a loopback round trip stops being cheaper than the bytes; over a real network the crossover is much higher, so this is the conservative end.

structs.name: ByteRange
structs.summary: `length` bytes starting at `offset`.
structs.description:
A negative `offset` means what it means to `read_range` — a suffix range,
"the last `length` bytes" — and is never coalesced, because where it lands
is not known until the length is.

structs.name: CoalescedPlan
structs.summary: How to answer `n` ranges with `len(fetches)` requests.
structs.description:
For each input range `i`: `group[i]` is the fetch it comes from, or -1 if
it has to be read on its own (a suffix or empty range), and `group_offset[i]`
is where inside that fetch its bytes begin.

traits.name: RangeReader
traits.summary: The one method coalescing needs. `InputFile` is a superset.

overloads.signature: def read_range(self, offset: Int, length: Int) -> List[UInt8]
def plan_ranges(ranges: List[ByteRange], max_gap: Int = Int(1048576)) -> CoalescedPlan
overloads.summary: Groups ranges that are adjacent, overlapping, or `max_gap` apart.
overloads.description:
The input order is preserved in the result — a caller that asked for the
footer last still gets the footer last — and ranges are sorted internally
only to find the groups.

overloads.signature: def read_ranges_coalesced[T: RangeReader](reader: T, ranges: List[ByteRange], max_gap: Int = Int(1048576)) -> List[List[UInt8]]
overloads.summary: Fetches the plan's groups one by one and slices the caller's ranges back out. Backends that can fetch groups at once do that instead and call `assemble`.

overloads.signature: def assemble[T: RangeReader](reader: T, plan: CoalescedPlan, ranges: List[ByteRange], var buffers: List[List[UInt8]]) -> List[List[UInt8]]
overloads.summary: The caller's ranges, in order, cut from `buffers` (one per fetch of `plan`). A range a fetch answers exactly gets that buffer, uncopied; a suffix or empty range, which no fetch covers, is read on its own.

modules.summary: `objectstore.s3` — an S3 client over `HttpClient`, signed with SigV4.
modules.description:
Covers what an Iceberg reader and writer actually issue: `GetObject` (with
`Range`, because a Parquet reader wants the footer before anything else),
`PutObject` (multipart above a threshold), `HeadObject`, `DeleteObject` and a
paginated `ListObjectsV2`.

Addressing works both ways. Virtual-host style (`bucket.s3.region.amazonaws.com`)
is what AWS prefers; path style (`endpoint/bucket/key`) is what MinIO, Ceph and
most S3-compatible servers default to, and what a bucket name with dots forces
even on AWS. `S3Config.path_style` picks, and a custom `endpoint` makes this
work against MinIO, R2 or anything else that speaks the protocol.

Credentials come from five places, in the order a caller should expect:
explicit properties, the `AWS_*` environment, the **EC2 instance role**
(IMDSv2, when neither of those set a key and no custom endpoint is
configured), REST-catalog **vended credentials** (which are just properties
under a location prefix — see `fileio.FileIOResolver`), and presigned URLs,
which carry the signature in the query string and need no credentials at the
point of use at all.

The instance role is what AWS SDKs fall back to as well. The shim does the
lookup and caches it for the process, "not on EC2" included, until five
minutes before the credentials expire. `AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true` turns
it off and `AWS_EC2_METADATA_SERVICE_ENDPOINT` points it elsewhere. From a
container, the instance's metadata hop limit must be at least 2.

aliases.name: MIN_PART_SIZE
aliases.summary: S3's floor for every part but the last. Not a suggestion: a smaller part is rejected at `CompleteMultipartUpload`, after the bytes have been sent.

aliases.name: DEFAULT_PART_SIZE
aliases.summary: Big enough that a 5 GB object stays inside the 10 000-part limit with room to spare, small enough that a failed part is cheap to resend.

structs.name: S3Config
structs.summary: Everything needed to address and sign against one S3 endpoint.

fields.name: endpoint
fields.summary: `https://minio.local:9000`, or `""` for the AWS regional endpoint.

fields.name: sign_payload
fields.summary: When false, `PUT` bodies are signed as `UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD` — a real option for a large object over TLS, where hashing the payload twice is pure overhead. Set from the `s3.unsigned-payload` property; default on, since dropping it also drops the guarantee that what S3 stored is what was signed.

fields.name: anonymous
fields.summary: Skip signing entirely: public buckets, and presigned URLs, need no credentials and are rejected by some servers if signed anyway.

fields.name: multipart_threshold
fields.summary: Objects larger than this go up as a multipart upload. 0 disables multipart entirely, which is the 0.1.x behaviour and still correct up to S3's 5 GB single-`PUT` ceiling.

fields.name: multipart_part_size
fields.summary: Bytes per part, clamped up to S3's 5 MiB floor.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, var endpoint: String, var region: String, path_style: Bool, var credentials: S3Credentials, sign_payload: Bool = True, anonymous: Bool = False, multipart_threshold: Int = Int(8388608), multipart_part_size: Int = Int(8388608))

overloads.summary: The standard `AWS_*` variables, plus `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL[_S3]`.
Iceberg property names, which is what a REST catalog hands back.
overloads.description:
Recognised: `s3.endpoint`, `s3.access-key-id`, `s3.secret-access-key`,
`s3.session-token`, `s3.region`, `s3.path-style-access`,
`s3.multipart.part-size-bytes` (Iceberg's own name and units),
`client.region` as a fallback for the region, and
`s3.unsigned-payload`.

Iceberg's `s3.multipart.threshold` is a *factor* of the part size
expressed as a decimal, which needs a float parser this module does
not have; the threshold follows the part size instead, and
`S3Config.multipart_threshold` sets it directly.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, var config: S3Config, var http: HttpClient)

overloads.summary: Retries per request; 3 by default, 0 to disable.
overloads.description:
The full policy — backoff window, ceiling, whether a non-idempotent
request may be repeated — is `self.http.retry`. S3 needs this more
than most callers do: `SlowDown` is how a bucket says "you are going
too fast", and it arrives at exactly the moment a scan is issuing its
hundredth range read.

overloads.signature: def url_for(self, bucket: String, key: String) -> Tuple[String, String, String]
overloads.summary: Returns `(url, host header value, signing path)`.
overloads.description:
The signing path is the request target *before* the query string, and
it must match byte for byte what the server reconstructs — hence
building it here rather than re-deriving it from the URL later.

overloads.signature: def request(self, method: String, bucket: String, key: String, params: List[QueryParam] = List(), body: Span[UInt8] = Span(), extra_headers: List[Header] = List(), range_start: Int = Int(-1), range_end: Int = Int(-1)) -> Response
def get_object(self, bucket: String, key: String, range_start: Int = Int(-1), range_end: Int = Int(-1)) -> List[UInt8]
overloads.summary: Whole object, or the inclusive byte range `[start, end]`.

overloads.signature: def signed_get(self, bucket: String, key: String, range_start: Int = Int(-1), range_end: Int = Int(-1)) -> BatchRequest
overloads.summary: A signed `GET` of the object or the inclusive range `[start, end]`, to send in a batch.

overloads.signature: def get_many(self, reqs: List[BatchRequest], what: List[String]) -> List[List[UInt8]]
overloads.summary: Runs signed `GET`s at once; raises naming `what[i]` for the first that failed.

overloads.signature: def get_ranges(self, bucket: String, key: String, ranges: List[Tuple[Int, Int]]) -> List[List[UInt8]]
overloads.summary: Several inclusive byte ranges `(start, end)` of one object, fetched at once.

overloads.signature: def head_object(self, bucket: String, key: String) -> Response
def object_length(self, bucket: String, key: String) -> Int
def object_exists(self, bucket: String, key: String) -> Bool
def put_object(self, bucket: String, key: String, body: Span[UInt8], content_type: String = "")
overloads.summary: Stores the object, as one `PUT` or as a multipart upload.
overloads.description:
The switch is `S3Config.multipart_threshold`. Nothing about the call
changes: `AnyOutputFile.overwrite` and `FileIOResolver.write` get
multipart for free, which is the point — a Parquet writer should not
have to know how big its own output turned out to be.

overloads.signature: def create_multipart_upload(self, bucket: String, key: String, content_type: String = "") -> String
overloads.summary: `POST /key?uploads` — returns the upload id.

overloads.signature: def upload_part(self, bucket: String, key: String, upload_id: String, part_number: Int, body: Span[UInt8]) -> String
overloads.summary: `PUT /key?partNumber=N&uploadId=…` — returns the part's ETag.
overloads.description:
Signed like any other request, so every part pays its own SigV4; with
`sign_payload = False` it pays `UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD` instead, which for a
multi-hundred-megabyte object over TLS is the difference between
hashing the data twice and hashing it once.

overloads.signature: def complete_multipart_upload(self, bucket: String, key: String, upload_id: String, etags: List[String])
overloads.summary: `POST /key?uploadId=…` with the part list, in order.

overloads.signature: def abort_multipart_upload(self, bucket: String, key: String, upload_id: String)
overloads.summary: `DELETE /key?uploadId=…`. Unaborted parts are billed until a lifecycle rule collects them, so this runs on every failure path.

overloads.signature: def put_object_multipart(self, bucket: String, key: String, body: Span[UInt8], content_type: String = "")
overloads.summary: Create, upload each part, complete — aborting if anything fails.
overloads.description:
Parts are `Span` slices of the caller's buffer, so the object is never
held twice: peak memory is the caller's own bytes plus one part's
worth of SigV4 hashing state.

overloads.signature: def delete_object(self, bucket: String, key: String)
def list_objects_v2(self, bucket: String, prefix: String = "", delimiter: String = "", max_keys: Int = Int(0), continuation_token: String = "") -> ListResult
overloads.summary: One page of `ListObjectsV2`. See `list_all` for every page.

overloads.signature: def list_all(self, bucket: String, prefix: String = "", delimiter: String = "") -> ListResult
overloads.summary: Every page, concatenated. Bounded at 10 000 requests so a server that keeps handing back the same token cannot spin forever.

overloads.signature: def presign_get(self, bucket: String, key: String, expires_seconds: Int = Int(3600)) -> String
overloads.summary: A URL that grants `GET` on one object for `expires_seconds`.
overloads.description:
Everything travels in the query string, so the holder needs no
credentials — which is the whole point, and why `HttpClient` keeps
redirects off: re-issuing a signed URL elsewhere would leak it.

overloads.summary: The EC2 instance role's credentials, or `None` off EC2, without a role, or with `AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true`.
The three characters that cannot appear in element text.
overloads.description:
Only `CompleteMultipartUpload` needs this, and only for an ETag, which in
practice is hex — but an ETag is server-chosen and this document decides
whether a 40 MB upload lands.

overloads.signature: def xml_element(body: String, tag: String, start: Int = Int(0)) -> Int
overloads.summary: Byte offset of `<tag>`'s content, or -1. Feeds `xml_text`.

overloads.signature: def xml_text(body: String, tag: String, start: Int = Int(0)) -> String
overloads.summary: The text of the first `<tag>` at or after `start`; `""` if absent.

overloads.signature: def xml_blocks(body: String, tag: String) -> List[String]
overloads.summary: Every `<tag>` … `</tag>` body, in document order.
`……` if that is what came back, else the first bytes of whatever did.
`s3://bucket/a/b` -> `("bucket", "a/b")`.
overloads.description:
`s3a://` and `s3n://` (the Hadoop schemes, still common in older Iceberg
metadata) address the same objects and are accepted here.

modules.summary: `objectstore.sigv4` — AWS Signature Version 4, header and query flavours.
modules.description:
Split out of `s3` because it is pure string algebra over `crypto`: given a
method, a path, query parameters, headers and a payload hash it produces the
canonical request, the string to sign, and the signature. That shape is what
makes it testable against the published `aws-sig-v4-test-suite` vectors
without a network or an S3 server anywhere in the picture.

Two callers use it: `S3Client`, which signs with an `Authorization` header,
and `presign_url`, which moves the same material into the query string so a
URL can be handed to something that knows nothing about AWS.

aliases.name: EMPTY_SHA256
aliases.summary: SHA-256 of the empty string — the payload hash of every bodyless request.

structs.name: QueryParam
structs.summary: One query parameter, **unencoded**. Signing encodes it.

structs.name: AmzTime
structs.summary: A signing timestamp in the two forms SigV4 needs.

fields.name: date_stamp
fields.summary: `20150830` — the date half of the credential scope.

overloads.summary: UTC calendar date from a Unix timestamp.
overloads.description:
Days-to-civil from Howard Hinnant's `chrono`-compatible algorithm: it
shifts the era so that leap days land at the end, which makes the
whole conversion branch-free integer arithmetic. Mojo has no calendar
library, and re-deriving this is cheaper than another FFI call.

overloads.summary: Reuses an `X-Amz-Date` value the caller already has (the test vectors, or a retried request that must keep its timestamp).

structs.name: SignedRequest
structs.summary: Everything a signing pass produced, so tests can check each stage.

overloads.summary: Seconds since the Unix epoch, via the FFI shim.
overloads.description:
Mojo's `std.time` offers only a monotonic clock, and SigV4 needs a real
UTC timestamp — AWS rejects requests more than 15 minutes out of skew.

overloads.signature: def canonical_path(path: String, normalize: Bool = False) -> String
overloads.summary: The canonical URI: each segment percent-encoded once, `/` left alone.
overloads.description:
`normalize` collapses `.`/`..` and duplicate slashes, which is what every
AWS service except S3 wants. **S3 signs the un-normalized path** — an S3
key may legitimately contain a literal `..` segment — so the S3 client
leaves this off.

overloads.summary: Encoded `k=v` pairs sorted by encoded name, then encoded value.
Returns `(canonical header block, signed header list)`.
overloads.description:
Names are lowercased and sorted; repeated names are joined with commas in
the order they appeared, per the SigV4 spec.

overloads.signature: def canonical_request(method: String, path: String, params: List[QueryParam], headers: List[Header], payload_hash: String, normalize: Bool = False) -> Tuple[String, String]
overloads.summary: Returns `(canonical request, signed headers)`.

overloads.signature: def credential_scope(date_stamp: String, region: String, service: String) -> String
def string_to_sign(amz_date: String, scope: String, canonical_req: String) -> String
def signing_key(secret_key: String, date_stamp: String, region: String, service: String) -> List[UInt8]
overloads.summary: The four-step HMAC ladder: date, region, service, `aws4_request`.

overloads.signature: def sign(secret_key: String, date_stamp: String, region: String, service: String, to_sign: String) -> String

def sign_request(method: String, path: String, params: List[QueryParam], headers: List[Header], payload_hash: String, access_key: String, secret_key: String, region: String, service: String, when: AmzTime, normalize: Bool = False) -> SignedRequest
overloads.summary: Header-flavoured SigV4.
overloads.description:
`headers` must already contain `host`, `x-amz-date` and, when a session
token is in play, `x-amz-security-token`: which headers are signed is the
caller's decision, and S3 in particular insists that
`x-amz-content-sha256` be among them.

overloads.signature: def presign_query(method: String, path: String, params: List[QueryParam], headers: List[Header], access_key: String, secret_key: String, session_token: String, region: String, service: String, when: AmzTime, expires_seconds: Int, normalize: Bool = False) -> String
overloads.summary: Query-flavoured SigV4: returns the full canonical query string, `X-Amz-Signature` included.
overloads.description:
The payload hash for a presigned URL is `UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD`: the point of
presigning is that whoever follows the URL never sees the credentials, so
they cannot be expected to hash a body the signer never had.
